beats.intro: Derivatives, module eight. [[sub]]What is an option worth before it expires, and what drives that value? This chapter looks at European options, which can only be exercised at maturity.
beats.exercise: [[a]]At any time before expiry, an option's price has two parts. The first is its exercise value: what it would be worth if it could be exercised right now. [[call]]For a call, that is the spot price minus the present value of the exercise price, or zero. [[put]]For a put, it is the present value of the exercise price minus the spot price, or zero. [[ex]]Take a one-year put with an exercise price of one thousand euros, and a rate of one percent. Six months in, the spot price is nine fifty. The present value of the exercise price is nine ninety-five oh four. [[res]]So the exercise value is forty-five euros and four cents.
beats.money: [[a]]Moneyness compares the spot price with the exercise price. [[call]]A call is in the money when the spot price is above the exercise price, at the money when equal, and out of the money when below. [[put]]For a put, it is the reverse. [[ex]]The put with a spot price of nine fifty and an exercise price of a thousand is in the money by fifty euros. [[sens]]Moneyness also drives sensitivity. A deep in-the-money option, very likely to be exercised, moves nearly one for one with the underlying. A deep out-of-the-money option barely moves. And near the money, small price changes decide whether the option is exercised.
beats.time: [[a]]The second part of an option's price is its time value: the price minus the exercise value. [[ex]]The put is trading at fifty euros. Its exercise value is forty-five oh four. [[res]]The time value is four euros ninety-six. [[why]]It is always positive, because a longer time, and more volatility, give the underlying more room to move in the option holder's favor. [[decay]]As maturity approaches, time value shrinks to zero, a process called time decay. At expiry, the price equals the payoff. [[atm]]Time value is largest when the option is at the money.
beats.bounds: [[a]]No arbitrage puts bounds on option prices. [[call]]A call can be worth no less than its exercise value, and no more than the underlying price. Nobody would pay more for the right to buy a share than the share itself. [[put]]A put can be worth no less than its exercise value, and no more than the exercise price. [[ex]]Take a call with an exercise price of a thousand euros, a one percent rate, and six months left. The underlying is at ten fifty. [[res]]The lower bound is fifty-four ninety-six. The upper bound is ten fifty. Any call price outside that range creates an arbitrage.
beats.replicate: [[a]]Replication works differently for options. A long forward can be copied by borrowing the present value of the forward price, and buying the underlying. The trade never needs to change. [[call]]A call is copied by buying the underlying and borrowing, but only a proportion of the present value of the exercise price. That proportion reflects the likelihood of exercise. [[adj]]As the underlying moves, and the option goes further in or out of the money, the proportion changes, so the replicating position must be adjusted over time. [[put]]A put is copied by selling the underlying short, and lending a proportion of the proceeds. [[end]]At expiry, if the call is exercised, the underlying is sold to repay the loan. If not, nothing more happens.
beats.factors: [[a]]Six factors drive an option's value. [[s]]The underlying price. A higher price helps a call, and hurts a put. [[x]]The exercise price. A higher exercise price hurts a call, and helps a put. [[t]]Time to expiration. More time usually helps both. For a put there is an exception: a longer wait lowers the present value of the payoff, so a deep in-the-money put can lose value. [[r]]The risk-free rate. A higher rate lowers the present value of the exercise price, so it helps a call and hurts a put. It does not directly affect time value. [[v]]Volatility. More volatility helps both calls and puts, because it widens the upside without changing the downside. [[i]]Income or cost of owning the underlying. Income, such as dividends, hurts a call and helps a put. Carry costs do the opposite.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]An option's price is its exercise value plus its time value, and time value decays to zero. [[w2]]Moneyness tells you how likely exercise is, and how sensitive the option is to the underlying. [[w3]]No arbitrage bounds a call between its exercise value and the underlying price, and a put between its exercise value and the exercise price. [[w4]]Replicating an option needs a changing position, unlike a forward.
beats.finish: Module eight complete. Next: put-call parity.
